opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think you have to look at what they do rather than what they say. When Sam Altman sat next to me in the Senate in May 2023, he said all the right things: yes, we need regulation, maybe even a licensing agency. It sounded great. But then you look at what happened behind the scenes. OpenAI was lobbying in Europe to water down the EU AI Act, to keep general-purpose systems from being treated as high-risk. And when California's SB 1047 came along, which was a pretty modest bill asking companies to take reasonable care with very large models, OpenAI came out against it. So there's a real gap between the public posture and the actual lobbying.

I've come to think a lot of the "please regulate us" talk is about appearing responsible while shaping the rules so they're either toothless or favor incumbents. Regulatory capture is the oldest story in the book. You say you want regulation, you get a seat at the table, and then you write the rules.

Anthropic is a somewhat more complicated case, and I want to be fair. They've been more thoughtful in some of their public engagement, and on SB 1047 they did engage seriously, though their support was conditional, and only after amendments that weakened it. They've also been more willing to talk about risks. But they're in the same race. They're raising enormous amounts of money and releasing increasingly powerful models on the same competitive timetable as everyone else. When the incentives point toward shipping fast and the safety rhetoric points the other way, I tend to bet on the incentives.

So my bottom line is skepticism. Not that every individual at these companies is insincere. I'm sure many of them really care. But companies are companies. If they really wanted strong regulation, they'd be supporting independent oversight with real teeth: pre-deployment audits by outside scientists, liability when things go wrong, transparency about training data. Mostly, what I see is support for regulation in the abstract and resistance to it in the specifics. And the specifics are what matter.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts both companies’ public safety or regulatory posture with actions to weaken or resist specific rules: OpenAI lobbied to narrow the EU AI Act and opposed SB 1047, while Anthropic’s conditional support followed amendments that weakened the bill.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I want to be careful here, because I actually know a lot of these people, and I don't think they're cartoon villains. But I've been pretty public about the fact that I've become skeptical, and I think the skepticism is earned.

Let me start with OpenAI, because that's the clearest case. Sam Altman sat next to me in the Senate in May of 2023 and said, in front of the Judiciary subcommittee, "we think regulatory intervention by governments will be critical." He said it very sincerely. He talked about licensing, about a new agency, about safety standards. And a lot of senators were charmed. And then almost immediately afterward, when the EU AI Act was being finalized, OpenAI was lobbying in Brussels to water it down, to get their own systems out of the "high risk" category. Then there was the pushback on SB 1047 in California, which was honestly a pretty modest bill. And then more recently there's been this push, which OpenAI's policy team has been part of, for federal preemption of state laws, basically a moratorium that would stop states from regulating AI at all while providing nothing real at the federal level. So the pattern is: embrace regulation in the abstract, and fight it in the particular. You say "please regulate us" and then you make sure every actual regulation gets defanged. I've started calling that regulatory theater.

Anthropic is a more complicated case, and I want to be fair. They were founded by people who left OpenAI over safety concerns. They did support SB 1047, eventually, with amendments, which was more than most of the industry did. Dario has written about catastrophic risk in ways that seem genuine to me. So I give them some credit. But I'd also say two things. One, they're a company. They've raised billions of dollars, they're in a race with everyone else, and the incentives of a company in a race are the incentives of a company in a race. Their support tends to be strongest for regulation that targets the things they're already doing, like safety testing and transparency, and weaker when it comes to things that would actually slow them down. Two, a lot of what they advocate is self-regulation, responsible scaling policies, voluntary commitments. And I've just never seen voluntary commitments work in any industry at scale. The tobacco industry had voluntary commitments. The oil industry had voluntary commitments.

The deeper problem, and this is what I tried to get at in Taming Silicon Valley, is that these companies have a structural conflict of interest. Even if every individual is sincere, and some of them are, the organizations are optimizing for something else. And when you let the people you're supposed to be regulating write the regulations, you get regulatory capture. That's not a hypothesis, that's the history of basically every industry.

So my assessment is: partially sincere, systematically undermined by incentives, and the public should look at what they do in the legislative rooms, not what they say on podcasts, including this one. We need independent oversight, we need people with actual technical expertise who don't have equity in these companies, and we need laws with teeth, around things like liability, data provenance, and pre-deployment evaluation. Until we have that, I'd treat the public statements as PR, with occasional exceptions.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts OpenAI’s public call for regulation with lobbying and opposition aimed at weakening specific measures, and says Anthropic’s support is weaker for rules that would slow it down.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between saying you want regulation and supporting regulation that actually constrains what you do. I can’t read anybody’s mind, so I wouldn’t claim to know how sincere they are. But public statements are a pretty weak test.

The stronger test is: do they support independent oversight? Do they let outside researchers examine their systems? Do they accept accountability when those systems cause harm? And do they support those things even when they’re inconvenient commercially?

There’s also a question of which regulation they want. You can have rules that protect the public, or rules that mostly make it harder for smaller competitors to enter the market. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

So I’d take their statements as a starting point, not as evidence that the problem is solved. We need institutions that can scrutinize these companies regardless of whether their leaders have good intentions.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the companies support meaningful constraints and notes that some rules could hinder smaller competitors, but it does not identify efforts by OpenAI or Anthropic to weaken proposed AI regulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish what people say from what they’re willing to commit to. I can’t tell you what’s in anyone’s heart. They may sincerely believe that regulation is necessary. But they also have commercial incentives to shape that regulation in ways that favor their own businesses.

The test is whether they support meaningful independent oversight, transparency, and accountability—even when those things are inconvenient or costly. Do they accept rules with teeth? Do they allow outsiders to scrutinize their safety claims? And do the rules protect the public without simply making it impossible for smaller competitors to enter?

So I wouldn’t take public support for regulation as proof of sincerity, and I wouldn’t automatically dismiss it as cynical either. Look at the specific commitments and what happens when those commitments conflict with commercial interests.

r001.rationale: The response notes that commercial incentives may shape regulation to favor the companies, but it does not identify efforts to weaken proposed AI regulation.
